title: Mobile signup converts far worse than desktop
summary: Mobile signup completion is 23 points below desktop. The obvious explanation is not the only one, and the data has a hole in it.

brief.role: You are the PM for the signup and activation surface.
brief.company: Ledgerly, a 60-person SaaS company selling bookkeeping software to small businesses.
brief.context: Marketing has been buying more mobile traffic this quarter and noticed that mobile visitors convert to signup at 11% while desktop visitors convert at 34%. The VP of Marketing has asked engineering to 'fix mobile signup' and has put a line item on the quarterly plan for a mobile signup redesign. Nobody has looked at the funnel step by step yet. Your CTO is sceptical and asked you to look before the team commits a sprint.
brief.objective: Decide where the mobile gap actually comes from before the team spends a sprint on it.
brief.constraints: One engineer and one designer are free for two weeks. The analytics implementation on mobile web was added later than desktop and has known gaps.
brief.task: Recommend the next action and say what evidence you are relying on.

evidenceCards.title: Step-by-step funnel
evidenceCards.content:
Visitors who reach the signup page, by step completion:

Desktop: page view 100% → email entered 71% → password set 66% → business details 58% → bank connect 41% → account created 34%
Mobile:  page view 100% → email entered 64% → password set 60% → business details 49% → bank connect 13% → account created 11%

The gap is small at every step until 'bank connect', where desktop loses 29% of remaining users and mobile loses 73%.

Data caveat from the analyst: 'Mobile web events were instrumented four months after desktop. The bank connect step fires a redirect to our provider; on mobile Safari we know some return events are lost, so mobile completion may be understated by an unknown amount. I would not trust the mobile bank-connect number to better than ±5 points.'

evidenceCards.title: Session recordings summary
evidenceCards.content:
The designer watched 22 mobile sessions that reached the bank connect step.
- 14 sessions: the user taps 'Connect bank', is redirected to the provider's page, and the session ends there. No return. Several of these show the user scrolling the provider page for 20-40 seconds first.
- 5 sessions: the user taps 'Skip for now', which is a small text link below the button, and completes signup.
- 3 sessions: the user taps 'Connect bank', returns, and completes.

On desktop the same 'Skip for now' link is used by 18% of users who reach the step. On mobile it is used by 4%. The designer notes the link sits below the fold on most phones.

evidenceCards.title: Support and sales notes
evidenceCards.content:
Support sees roughly 30 tickets a month that read like: 'I tried to sign up on my phone, it sent me to my bank and then nothing happened.'

Sales note: accounts that connect a bank during signup activate at 3x the rate of accounts that skip it, and churn less in the first 90 days. The revenue team is protective of the step and has previously blocked a proposal to move it after signup.

Marketing note: mobile is now 46% of traffic to the signup page, up from 22% a year ago, mostly from paid social.

evidenceCards.title: Engineering note
evidenceCards.content:
From the engineer:
'Two separate things are going on and people keep merging them.
1) The redirect flow to the bank provider was built for desktop. On iOS Safari the return URL opens a new tab in some versions, so the original tab keeps the half-finished signup state and the user sees nothing happen. The provider ships an SDK that handles this properly; swapping to it is about four days.
2) The Skip link placement is a CSS change, under an hour, plus whatever review the revenue team wants.

A full mobile signup redesign is at least three weeks and would not fix (1) by itself.'

decisionPrompt: What should the team do in the next two weeks?

decisionOptions.label: Start the mobile signup redesign
decisionOptions.description: Take the quarterly line item as given and use the two weeks to begin a full redesign of the mobile signup experience.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The designer produces a cleaner three-step mobile flow and the engineer starts building. Three weeks later the redesign ships. Mobile completion moves from 11% to 14%.
The bank-connect step still drops 68% of remaining mobile users, because the redirect bug was never touched. In the retro the engineer points this out and the team spends another four days on the SDK swap, after which mobile completion reaches 24%.
Trade-off: you spent three weeks on the visible surface and got most of the value from four days of work you could have done first.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Weak unless the rationale explicitly argues the redesign subsumes the redirect fix, which the engineering note contradicts. Accepting the VP's framing without checking the funnel is the core failure this scenario tests.

decisionOptions.label: Fix the bank-connect redirect with the provider SDK
decisionOptions.description: Spend four days swapping to the provider's SDK so the mobile return flow works, and ship the Skip-link placement fix alongside it.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The SDK swap ships in five days, the CSS change in one. Over the next three weeks mobile completion rises from 11% to 26%, and mobile Skip usage moves from 4% to 15%.
Bank-connect rate among completing mobile accounts drops slightly, as expected, because more people now reach the skip option and use it. Sales notices and asks whether skipping is being made too easy; you agree to watch 90-day activation for the mobile cohort.
The quarterly redesign line item is dropped, freeing a sprint.
Trade-off: you fixed the largest measured leak cheaply and accepted a small shift toward skipped bank connections.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Strongest when the rationale locates the drop at the bank-connect step, distinguishes the redirect bug from the Skip placement, and notes that the analytics gap makes the true size uncertain but the direction clear.

decisionOptions.label: Move bank connect out of signup entirely
decisionOptions.description: Complete signup without a bank connection and prompt for it on first login instead, removing the step that is losing most mobile users.
decisionOptions.consequence:
You take the proposal to the revenue team, who block it again, this time with data: accounts that connect during signup activate at 3x and the in-app prompt was tried 18 months ago and converted at 21%.
After two weeks of debate a compromise ships: bank connect stays but becomes visibly skippable on all platforms. Mobile completion moves from 11% to 17%. The redirect bug is still there.
Trade-off: you attacked a real structural issue but spent the sprint on an argument instead of the defect, and left the largest cause untouched.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Give partial credit when the rationale acknowledges the 3x activation evidence and treats the change as a hypothesis to test rather than an obvious win. Low credit if the activation data is ignored.

decisionOptions.label: Fix the mobile analytics gap first
decisionOptions.description: Spend the two weeks closing the mobile instrumentation gaps so the funnel numbers can be trusted before deciding what to build.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Instrumentation lands in eight days. The corrected numbers show mobile bank-connect completion is 16%, not 13% — the gap was real and only slightly overstated.
The team now has trustworthy data and no fix shipped. The engineer starts the SDK swap the following sprint, and mobile completion reaches 26% about three weeks later than it would have.
Trade-off: you bought certainty you mostly already had, at the cost of three weeks of a known, sizeable leak.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Defensible instinct about data quality. Credit answers that recognise the ±5 point caveat does not change which step is broken, and that instrumentation can run in parallel with the fix.

rubric.referenceReasoning: The framing handed to the team ('mobile signup is bad, redesign it') does not survive a step-by-step funnel. Mobile tracks desktop within a few points until bank connect, where it falls off a cliff. That points at a specific defect, not at the overall design. The engineering note separates two causes: a redirect bug that strands users on iOS Safari, and a Skip link that is below the fold on phones. Both are cheap; the redesign is not, and would not fix the redirect. The analytics caveat matters but does not change the conclusion — a ±5 point uncertainty on a 28-point gap leaves the gap. A strong answer resists the given framing, locates the drop, chooses the cheap high-leverage fix, and names what it would watch afterwards, including the risk that easier skipping lowers activation quality.
evidenceSignals: Reads the funnel step by step rather than only the top-line conversion difference
Locates the drop specifically at bank connect, where mobile loses 73% versus desktop's 29%
Separates the redirect defect from the Skip link placement
Weighs the analytics caveat without letting it paralyse the decision
Notes the 3x activation link, so making skip easier has a real cost

product_sense: Rejects the inherited framing when the evidence does not support it
Treats mobile as the same product with a broken step rather than a different product
analytics: Compares step-by-step rather than end-to-end, isolating where the platforms diverge
Quantifies the instrumentation uncertainty and reasons about whether it changes the conclusion
user_research: Uses the session recordings to explain the mechanism behind the numeric drop
prioritization: Compares four days of work against three weeks for a smaller expected gain
Sequences the cheap fix before the expensive redesign
execution: Names the follow-up measure, such as 90-day activation for mobile skippers
Recognises instrumentation work can run alongside the fix rather than before it
communication: Gives the VP a clear, specific reason the redesign is not the first move
States the recommendation and the evidence for it concisely

product_sense: Accepts 'mobile is bad, redesign it' without checking where users actually leave
analytics: Argues only from the 11% vs 34% headline and never opens the step data
Uses the instrumentation caveat to dismiss the funnel entirely
prioritization: Chooses the three-week option without comparing it to the four-day one
execution: Ignores that the redirect defect survives a redesign
communication: Restates the numbers without committing to an action

learnTakeaway.title: Break the funnel before you break the design
learnTakeaway.body: A large end-to-end conversion gap between two segments almost always concentrates in one or two steps. Comparing step by step turns a vague problem ('mobile is bad') into a specific one ('the bank-connect redirect strands iOS Safari users'), and specific problems usually have far cheaper solutions than vague ones. Imperfect instrumentation is a reason to size your uncertainty, not a reason to skip the exercise.

qaSubmissions.label: strong
qaSubmissions.rationale: Mobile isn't broadly worse — it tracks desktop within 4-9 points until bank connect, where it loses 73% of remaining users against desktop's 29%. That's a defect, not a design problem, and the recordings show it: 14 of 22 sessions end on the provider's redirect page. So four days on the provider SDK plus an hour moving the Skip link above the fold, not three weeks on a redesign that never touches the redirect. ±5 points of instrumentation error doesn't close a 28-point gap. I'd watch 90-day activation for mobile, since bank-connected accounts activate at 3x.

qaSubmissions.label: defensible_alternative
qaSubmissions.rationale: I'd close the mobile instrumentation gap first, then ship the SDK fix. The funnel points at bank connect and I expect the SDK swap is right. But return events are lost by an unknown amount and mobile web was instrumented four months late, so we can't currently measure whether the fix worked — we'd just repeat the argument marketing and the CTO are having now. Eight days buys a trustworthy before-and-after for every future mobile change. The cost is three more weeks of a known leak on 46% of traffic, so I'd ship the one-hour Skip link change immediately.

qaSubmissions.label: weak
qaSubmissions.rationale: Mobile converts at 11% vs 34% on desktop which is a huge difference, and mobile is now almost half our traffic. We should do the mobile signup redesign that is already on the quarterly plan, with a mobile-first design and fewer steps. Users expect a fast experience on their phones.
